INTERESTS OF AMICUS CURIAE1
Amicus curiae Global Action on Gun Violence
(“GAGV”) is a non-profit organization dedicated to
reducing gun violence in the U.S. and the world using
litigation, human-rights advocacy, and research, with
a focus on stopping cross-border gun trafficking.
GAGV represents and assists the Government of
Mexico to stop the trafficking of firearms—including
assault rifles—from the U.S. to the cartels.  GAGV has
presented reports and testimony at the Organization
of American States, the Inter-American Commission
for Human Rights, United Nations bodies, and
international conferences.
INTRODUCTION AND STATEMENT
On December 14, 2012, a gunman walked into Sandy
Hook Elementary School in Newtown, Connecticut,
carrying a semi-automatic AR-15 assault rifle.  Within
five minutes, he fired 154 rounds, murdering twenty
children and six adults.
On November 4, 2019, cartel gunmen in Mexico’s
Sonora desert fired 1,893 bullets on a three-car convoy
en route to a wedding, massacring nine dual U.S.-
Mexican citizens, including six children.  Two of the
firearms recovered and traced from the LeBaron
Massacre were, like the Sandy Hook gunman’s, assault
rifles sold in the U.S.  Mónica Romero, Inside the
LeBarón Massacre in Mexico: US-Purchased Rifles and
1,893 Rounds, EL PAÍS (Nov. 8, 2025, at 23:40 EST),

Neither massacre was an aberration.  Modeled after
military weapons and engineered to maximize casualties, “assault weapons” have been used to perpetrate
many of the deadliest mass casualty events in modern
U.S. history.  The human toll of even a small fraction
of these attacks is staggering: 21 killed in a Uvalde,
Texas elementary school; 10 in a Buffalo, New York
supermarket; 10 in a Boulder, Colorado supermarket;
9 in a Dayton, Ohio bar; 23 in an El Paso, Texas Wal-
Mart; 11 in a Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania synagogue; 17
in a Parkland, Florida high school; 26 in a Sutherland
Springs, Texas church; 49 in an Orlando, Florida
nightclub; 60 at a Las Vegas, Nevada music festival; 7
at a 4th of July parade in Highland Park, Illinois.
In Mexico, after the U.S. federal Assault Weapons
Ban expired in 2004, U.S.-sold assault rifles became
a weapon of choice for cartels.  These trafficked rifles
are routinely used to commit murders, perpetrate
massacres, attack law enforcement and military
personnel, and intimidate civilian populations.  By
enabling cartels to project violence and fear, assault
rifles trafficked from the U.S. contribute to widespread
insecurity, displacement, migration into the United
States, and cross-border drug-trafficking operations.
Assault weapons are sought after by mass killers
and transnational criminal organizations because
they are catastrophic force multipliers, giving shooters
the benefit of rapid firepower while depriving victims
of time to flee and first responders of time to intervene.
To protect their residents and prevent further mass
casualty atrocities, Connecticut and Cook County,
Illinois prohibited the sale, transfer, and possession of
assault weapons (together, the “Statutes”).

3
Petitioners would have the Court hold that the
Second Amendment enshrines a right to possess
these specific destructive ri fles, so long as they are
sufficiently popular.  But th e Bill of Rights does not
consecrate a right to any specific weapons on the basis
of popularity or otherwise.  And neither Heller nor
Bruen should be read as placing a constitutional
imprimatur on weapons of such extraordinarily deadly
force.
Although the Framers did not face anything
resembling modern guns or gun violence, they were
nonetheless circumspect about firearms, and foundingera laws reflected common-sense prohibitions on the
sale and use of “dangerous and unusual” weapons.
District of Columbia v. Heller , 554 U.S. 570 (2008),
departed from nearly 230 years of precedent in holding
that the Second Amendment protects individuals’
right to possess a handgun in the home for lawful selfdefense purposes.  But even as it did so, the Court tied
that right to weapons “in common use at the time,”
recognizing “the historical tradition of prohibiting the
carrying of ‘dangerous and unusual weapons’” as a
settled limit on the individual right to keep and bear
arms.  Id. at 627.
New York State Rifle & Pistol Ass’n v. Bruen, 597
U.S. 1 (2022), altered the paradigm.  While Bruen
ostensibly did not disturb Heller’s “common use” test,
it rejected the means-end scrutiny that lower courts
applied after Heller and required the government to
show that a challenged regulation is “consistent with
this Nation’s historical tradition of firearm
regulation.”  Id. at 17.
While the challenged Statutes are properly regulated
under Bruen, that test is ill-suited to modern weapons.
Bruen itself acknowledged that “dramatic technologi-

4
cal changes” may call for a more nuanced approach, id.
at 27, and United States v. Rahimi , 602 U.S. 680, 692
(2024), confirmed that courts should look to the principles underlying historical regulation, not demand a
“historical twin.”
Petitioners overlook that caveat and, to establish
constitutional protection for assault rifles, seek to take
Heller and Bruen one step further.  They argue that,
notwithstanding their inherent dangerousness, assault
weapons are constitutionally protected because they
are “in common use.”  Petitioners’ argument distorts
Heller’s phrase, which tied commonality to whether
guns are possessed by law-abiding citizens for lawful
purposes.  But the record here does not support that
finding for assault weapons.  Indeed, Petitioners rely
on sales figures and surveys that include significant
numbers of assault rifles sold in the U.S. and
ultimately trafficked to cartels in Mexico.  That cannot
support constitutional enshrinement.  Petitioners’
interpretation also risks making popularity the litmus

Deborah Azrael & Matthew Miller,  The Number and
Type of Private Firearms in the United States , 704
ANNALS Am. Acad. Pol. & Soc. Sci. 70, 77 (2022).  The
concentration of firearms in the hands of a small
number of Americans is highly relevant.  Even tens of
millions of assault weapons held in the arsenals of a
few would be uncommon, like model trains sold
exclusively to not-so-common, not-so-usual enthusiasts.
That niche firearm enthusiasts amass assault weapons
does not mean those firearms are “in common use” and
certainly does not entitle them to constitutional
protection.
In addition, Petitioners point to gun manufacturer
surveys (again, from the NSSF), that fail to report how
many manufactured weapons were sold to consumers–

21
–and fail to account for demand driven by criminal
organizations.  See NSSF, Firearm Production in the
United States with Firearm Import and Export Data 7
(2023), https://perma.cc/P6A8-DZK2.  Manufacturer
data further shows that historical production of semiautomatic rifles constitutes just 11% of overall firearm
production.  See NSSF 2025 Production Figures.  Even
that number may be decreasing; AR-15 production has
declined by over 60% since 2021.  See NSSF, NSSF
Releases Most Recent Fi rearm Production Figures
(Jan. 15, 2026), https://www.nssf.org/articles/nssf-relea
ses-most-recent-firearm-production-figures-3/.
Petitioners also rely heavily on a William English
survey that has been criticized for its methodology and
findings.  See Deborah Azrael et al., A Critique of
Findings on Gun Ownership, Use and Imagined Use
from the 2021 National Firearms Survey: Response to
William English , 78 SMU L. Rev. 239 (2025).  The
English survey did not ask survey participants about
the number of AR-style rifles currently owned, but
instead how many each participant ever owned, failing
to account for weapons that were once owned but then
destroyed, sold, or otherwise transferred.  Id. at 243,
250.  Certain survey participants also may have been
classified as gun owners when they were not.  Id. at
247.  As numerous statisticians have noted, survey
evidence verifying gun ownership is inherently
unreliable, because, among other things, it relies on a
self-selected minority of responders who presumably
would not include individuals planning to use weapons
for criminal purposes.  See David Hemenway, Survey
Research and Self-Defense Gun Use: An Explanation of
Extreme Overestimates, 87 J. Crim. L. & Criminology
1430 (1997); Philip J. Cook & Jens Ludwig, Defensive
Gun Uses: New Evidence from a National Survey, 14 J.
Quantitative Criminology 111 (1998).

22
Even taken at face value, Petitioners’ cited survey
evidence indicates that just 6% of U.S. adults own AR-
15-style assault weapons, hardly amounting to
“common use.”  See Washington Post-Ipsos Poll of 2104
Gun Owners , Ipsos (Oct. 2022) https://www.ipsos.
com/sites/default/files/ct/news/documents/2023-03/Wa
shington%20Post-Ipsos%20AR-15%20Polling.pdf (20%
of gun owners reported owning an AR-15-style firearm);
Emily Guskin, Why do Americans own AR-15s? ,
Washington Post (Mar. 27, 2023), https://www.washing
tonpost.com/nation/interactive/2023/american-ar-15-gunowners/ (noting that this number equals 6% of adults).
Even the English survey puts the figure no higher
than 10%—again, not “common use.”  See William
English, 2021 National Firearms Survey: Updated
Analysis Including Types of Firearms Owned 1–2 (Geo.
Univ. McDonough Sch. Of Bus., Rsch. Paper No.
4109494, 2022), https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.
cfm?abstract_id=4109494 (reporting that, of the 31.9%
of respondents that own a firearm, 30.2% of that
subset reported having owned an AR-15-style firearm).
Petitioners’ and their amici’s evidence fails to show
that assault weapons are common and to exclude
assault weapons purchased for criminals, including
cartels in Mexico.  No Second Amendment inquiry
should credit firearm sales to criminals.
II. Bruen’s Framework Is Particularly Ill-
Suited to Assault Weapons and Should Be
Reconsidered.
Although the Statutes are unquestionably constitutional under Heller, Bruen, and their progeny, this case
presents a unique opportunity for the Court to
reconsider and revise Bruen’s test, at least as it applies
to assault weapons.

23
To begin, “a framework that relies exclusively on
text, history, and tradition to adjudicate Second
Amendment claims provides only the aura, but not the
reality, of objectivity.”  Duncan v. Bonta, 19 F.4th 1087,
1118 (9th Cir. 2021) (Berzon, J., concurring); see also
Emily Bazelon, How “History and Tradition” Rulings
Are Changing American Law , N.Y. Times Mag. (Apr.
29, 2024), https://www.nytimes.com/2024/04/29/maga
zine/history-tradition-law-conservative-judges.html
(reporting Justice Barrett’s acknowledgment that a
judge’s hunt for historical sources could be like
“looking over a crowd and picking out your friends”).
Judges, who are not historians, are forced to either
abstract an 18th-century pe digree for a modern
regulation or declare an entire category of publicsafety regulations constitutionally untouchable.  See
Bruen, 597 U.S. at 107, 113 (Breyer, J., dissenting).  The
result is a one-way ratchet: the Second Amendment
protects an ever-larger scope of 21st-century “arms”
while tying the government’s authority to a fixed
catalog of now-antiquated 18th- and 19th-century
statutes that regulated far less-dangerous weapons.
Although the Court has stated that Bruen’s history
and tradition test is neither a regulatory straitjacket
nor a means of “trapp[ing] [laws] in amber,” United
States v. Rahimi, 602 U.S. 680, 691 (2024), that
assurance provides limited guidance and little solace.
Regardless of how liberally one construes a distant
past, finding an analogue for a type of weaponry that
was inconceivable at the Founding—to say nothing of
locating an analogue to the modern laws regulating
it—is a herculean task.  And, once a court identifies a
regulation that can serve as an analogue, Bruen
provides no guidance as to whether it should be used
as an analogue, suggesting, instead, that courts may
discount laws that are too old, too recent, too

24
discriminatory, or simply too anomalous.  See Bruen,
597 U.S. at 46 (discounting three of the government’s
proposed colonial-era analogues in part because it
“doubt[ed] that [just] three colonial regulations could
suffice to show a tradition of public carry regulation”);
Rahimi, 602 U.S. at 746 (Jackson, J., concurring)
(noting the majority failed to clarify “[h]ow many
analogues add up to a tradition”).
Bruen has spawned divergent outcomes “on virtually
every consequential Second Amendment issue” decided
in its wake.  Rahimi, 602 U.S. at 741–43 (Jackson, J.,
concurring); see also Joseph Blocher & Eric Ruben,
Originalism-by-Analogy and Second Amendment
Adjudication, 133 Yale L. J. 99, 105–06 (2023)
(cataloguing “unpredictable case outcomes” following
Bruen); Jacob D. Charles, The Dead Hand of a Silent
Past: Bruen, Gun Rights, and the Shackles of History ,
73 Duke L. J. 67, 145 (2023) (courts have devised
“bespoke subrules” to imp lement Bruen); Clara Fong,
Kelly Percival & Thomas Wolf, Judges Find the
Supreme Court’s Bruen Test Unworkable, Brennan Ctr.
for Just. (June 26, 2023), https://www.brennan
center.org/our-work/research-reports/judges-find-supr
eme-courts-bruen-test-unworkable.  This pattern is
neither temporary nor fixable by lower courts.
Rahimi, 602 U.S. at 741 (Jackson, J., concurring)
(“Make no mistake: Today’s effort to clear up the [post-
Bruen] ‘misunderst[andings],’ is a tacit admission that
lower courts are struggling.   In my view, the blame
may lie with us, not with them.” (citation modified)).
Rather, the indeterminacy Bruen has caused will exist
for as long as the Court ma ndates a test with no
settled evidentiary threshold and no principled
account of how much similarity is enough.

25
A. Bruen Is Unworkable When Applied to
Assault Weapons.
Bruen’s history and tradition methodology, though
infirm in any context, collapses when applied to
assault weapons because no such weapons existed in
the founding era.
1. There Were No Firearms Remotely
Analogous to Modern Assault
Weapons During the Founding Era.
Bruen instructs courts to look to the founding era
without precisely defining that era, leaving lower
courts to vacillate between 1791, when the Second
Amendment was ratified, and 1868, when the
Fourteenth Amendment incorporated the Bill of
Rights against the States.  Bruen, 597 U.S. at 38.
Neither era, though, had firea rms that were effective
mass killing tools and availa ble to civilians—so there
was no legislative impetus to ban them.
Early American firearms were primitive by modern
standards.  Although, by 1791, the cumbersome matchlock ignition system chara cteristic of seventeenthcentury firearms had largely been replaced by the
flintlock, flintlocks were, like all muzzle-loaders of the
era, “liable to misfire” and glacially slow to reload,
making them “awkward tools either for perpetrating
or resisting crimes of passion.”  Brian DeLay, The Myth
of Continuity in American Gun Culture , 113 Cal. L.
Rev. 1, 15, 22, 25, 32 (2025) (citing Hew Strachan,
European Armies and the Conduct of War 16–17 (1983)).
Between 1791 and 1868, firearms technology progressed, but not to a point where it resembled
anything approaching a modern assault weapon.
The first practical repeating handguns—Colt-style
revolvers and multi-barrel “pepperboxes”—were more

26
practical than eighteenth-century muskets, but the
majority held seven or fewer rounds, and the three
revolvers produced in the nineteenth century holding
more than ten rounds were so “extraordinarily
unusual and made in tiny quantities” that they are
“best characterized as ‘experimental.’”  Id. at 37–38;
see also id. at 26 (citing Joseph Bradley, Guns for the
Tsar: American Technology and The Small Arms
Industry in Nineteenth-Century Russia, 12–19 (1990)).
Even these more advanced guns were cumbersome to
use: each chamber had to be charged with powder,
loaded with a ball, rammed, and then capped by hand,
such that reloading a six-sh ot revolver could take a
minute and a half or more.  Id. at 38.  The result was
a glacial rate of fire—a sharp contrast to the AR-15
used, for example, in the Parkland, Florida high school
shooting, which discharged at a rate of 1.5 rounds per
second, or 90 shots per minute, faster than the 12 to
15 rounds per minute rate that the military trains
soldiers to fire.  See C.J. Chivers et al., With AR-15s,
Mass Shooters Attack wit h the Rifle Firepower
Typically Used by Infantry Troops  (Feb. 28, 2018),
https://www.nytimes.com/interactive/2018/02/28/us/ar
-15-rifle-mass-shootings.html.
Even the first reliable large-capacity firearms, the
Henry rifle (1860) and the Winchester Model 1866,
were “relatively slow to load”: they had fixed
magazines, the shooter cycled the action by hand to
eject each casing and chamber the next round, and an
empty magazine had to be refilled one round at a time.
DeLay, supra, at 39–40, 42, 44.  They were also scarce
and hardly a cause for legislative action: of the
approximately 9,000 that were not shipped to foreign
militaries and remained for the domestic market, more
than 90% went to Union soldiers during the Civil War.
Id. at 41.

27
In short, no firearm in existence prior to 1868
remotely resembled a modern assault rifle, and
certainly none that “functioned well enough to become
militarily and commercially significant” at any point
before the nineteenth century.  Id. at 15.  Relatedly,
there were not barrages of public massacres using
anything akin to modern assault weapons until late in
the twentieth century, obviating any legislative
impetus to ban or restrict them.
2. Bruen’s Historical Analogue Test
Does Not Work When Applied to
Assault Weapons.
The absence of a founding- era firearm akin to a
modern assault weapon should have no bearing on
modern legislatures’ ability to regulate the technology.
Governments legislate for existing problems, not
existential ones.  Although America had a “diverse,
extensive, and sometimes deeply intrusive tradition of
regulating firearms in the name of public safety,” no
founding era law regulated the use of a type of
firearm—assault weapons—that would have been
inconceivable to generation s of musket and pistolwielding Americans.  See DeLay, supra, at 35.  Instead,
the laws enacted before 1868 make clear that when
Americans did regulate guns, they did so because of
their public safety risk and without regard to their
perceived “commonality.”
Virginia, for example, prohibited “armed” men
from engaging in terrorizing conduct in public places.
An Act Forbidding and Punishing Affrays, ch. 49,
1786 Va. Acts 35.  Massachusetts prohibited people
from gathering while “armed with clubs, or other
weapons.”  An Act to Prevent Routs, Riots, and

28
Tumultuous Assemblies, and the Evil Consequences
Thereof, ch. 8, 1786 Mass. Acts 502, 502–503.
An 1813 Louisiana law criminalized carrying “any
concealed weapon, such as a dirk, dagger, knife, [or]
pistol.”  An Act Against Carrying Concealed Weapons,
and Going Armed in Public Places in an Unnecessary
Manner, 1813 La. Acts 172, 172–75.  An 1837 Georgia
law made it unlawful to “sell” or “keep” most types of
“pistols.”  An Act to Guard and Protect the citizens of
this State, Against the Unwarrantable and too
Prevalent Use of Deadly Weapons, 1837 Ga. Laws 90,
90–91.  An 1831 Indiana law prohibited any person
other than a “traveller” from “wear[ing] or carry[ing] a
dirk, pistol, sword in a cane, or other dangerous
weapon concealed.”  An Act Relative to Crime and
Punishment, ch. 26, 1831 Ind. Acts 180, 192.  And a
New Mexico law in the 1860s barred “any class of
pistols whatever.”  An Act Prohibiting Carrying of
Weapons Concealed or Ot herwise, ch. 61, 1864–65
N.M. Laws 406, 406–08.  In all, scholars have
catalogued roughly 760 early laws regulating the use
and storage of firearms, each of which was aimed at
curbing the use of dangerous weapons regardless of
their perceived popularity.  Robert J. Spitzer, Gun Law
History in the United States and Second Amendment
Rights, 80 L. & Contemp. Probs. 55, 61 (2017).
But no founding era regulation restricted anything
akin to assault weapons because “repeating firearms
and high-capacity weapons were much too rare and too
irrelevant to public safety to attract regulatory
attention.”  DeLay, supra, at 35; cf. Spitzer, supra, at
68–69 (explaining that new firearm technologies drew
regulation not when they were invented but rather
once they began to circulate widely).  However, one can

29
safely assume from the myriad gun laws that had been
enacted in the founding era, that if legislatures had
confronted repeated atrocities akin to the massacre at
Sandy Hook, they would have regulated assault
weapons just as they regulated the knives and
primitive firearms then available.
Elevating the absence of law to a nearly inviolate
entitlement supersedes a host of inalienable rights,
including the right to life and the rights to assemble,
speak, and exist safely in public spaces.  See Jonathan
Lowy & Kelly Sampson, The Right Not To Be Shot:
Public Safety, Private Guns, and the Constellation of
Constitutional Liberties, 14 Georgetown J. L. & Pub.
Pol’y 187, 190 (2016) (presenting the right to life as a
“counterweight” to Second Amendment rights).  It
also defies the longstanding common law adapting
constitutional rights to protect public safety.  As
Justice Breyer noted in his Bruen dissent, “I believe
the Amendment allows States to take account of the
serious problems posed by gun violence. . . . [and] I fear
that the Court’s interpretation ignores these significant dangers and leaves States without the ability to
address them.”  Bruen, 597 U.S. at 91 (Breyer, J.,
dissenting); see also Eric Ruben, Rosanna Smart & Ali
Rowhani-Rahbar, One Year Post-Bruen: An Empirical
Assessment, 110 Va. L. Rev. Online 20 (2024)
(documenting hundreds of decisions relying on Bruen
to invalidate various gun laws).  Surely, the Founders
would have feared this, too.
B. Bruen’s Carve-Out for “Unprecedented”
and “Dramatic” Changes Is a More
Apt Test.
Bruen’s majority acknowledged that history and
tradition may not be appropriate benchmarks in every
instance, and that “cases implicating unprecedented

30
societal concerns or dramatic technological changes
may require a more nuanced approach.”  Bruen, 597
U.S. at 27.  Although Bruen endorsed this carve-out,
the majority was, respectfully, wrong to allude to it as
a last resort.  Given that virtually all modern firearm
regulations involve “unprecedented societal concerns”—
mass shootings, extremist violence, and cross-border
trafficking—stemming from “dramatic” technological
changes—ghost guns, 3D-printed firearms, highcapacity magazines, and semiautomatic rifles—the
“nuanced approach” should be the sum of the analysis.
See Samantha Barrera, Note, Unreason by Analogy:
Principle over Pedanticism and the Nuanced Approach
to Bruen, 67 Ariz. L. Rev. 517 (2025).
A “nuanced approach” does not have to mean a “new”
approach.  Indeed, before Bruen, every lower court
used a nuanced, fact-specific approach, assessing
compelling and substantial government interests and
ensuring that challenged legislation was reasonably
related to legislators’ stated aims.  See Kolbe v. Hogan,
849 F.3d 114, 139 (4th Cir. 2017); Worman v. Healey,
922 F.3d 26, 39 (1st Cir. 2019); Ass’n of N.J. Rifle &
Pistol Clubs, Inc. v. Att’y Gen. N.J., 910 F.3d 106, 117
(3d Cir. 2018); N.Y. State Rifle & Pistol Ass’n v. Cuomo,
804 F.3d 242, 261 (2d Cir. 2015).  This approach is both
flexible and pragmatic, allowing legislatures to
address gun violence through tailored, evidence-based
solutions rather than by anachronism.  See Stephen
Breyer, Pragmatism or Textualism, 138 Harv. L. Rev.
717, 769 (2025); Nelson Lund, Second Amendment
Originalism, “General Law, ” and Rahimi’s Two-Fold
Failure, 78 SMU L. Rev. 459, 489 (2025).  And, as many
courts of appeals have determined, regulations
prohibiting possession, ownership, sale, or transfer of

31
assault weapons amply meet that standard. 6  See
Kolbe, 849 F.3d at 139; Worman, 922 F.3d at 39; Ass’n
of N.J. Rifle & Pistol Clubs , 910 F.3d at 117; Cuomo ,
804 F.3d at 261.
Adopting a “nuanced” approach would not increase
the discretion Bruen expressly sought to remove any
more than Bruen and its progeny have created
unpredictability and discretion in applying the history
and tradition test.  If anything, the Bruen test’s
reliance on analogy grants courts wider discretion,
risking unprincipled and results-driven jurisprudence.
See Vidal v. Elster, 602 U.S. 286, 324 (2024) (Barrett,
J., concurring) (a “rule rendering tradition dispositive
is itself a judge-made test”).
Despite what Bruen ostensibly set out to do, its
practical effect was to concentrate gun rights
policymaking “in one place: the Supreme Court.”  Mark
A. Lemley, The Imperial Supreme Court, 136 Harv. L.
Rev. F. 97, 97 (2022).  The irony is that vesting the
judiciary with this type of power would have been
anathema in a founding era in which courts generally
deferred to legislatures, making Bruen’s history and
tradition test decidedly untraditional.  See William
Michael Treanor, Judicial Review Before Marbury , 58
Stan. L. Rev. 455, 557 (2005); Saul A. Cornell, The
Police Power and the Authority to Regulate Firearms in
Early America, Brennan Ctr. for Just. (2021), https://
www.brennancenter.org/sites/default/files/2021-06/Co
rnell_final.pdf.  Means-end scrutiny, by contrast,
returns “policy” judgments to where “history and

because the Bruen historical analogue test would be equally
unworkable in those instances.

32
tradition” deposited them: in the hands of the
legislature.  See Bernadette Meyler, Fiction at the
Court, 138 Harv. L. Rev. F. 22, 36–37 (2024).

For the foregoing reasons, the Court should find
that the Statutes are cons titutional and use this
opportunity to develop a workable framework for the
challenges posed by assault weapons.
